questions.title: On exposure to cold, all listed responses occur
questions.question: On exposure to cold:

options.A: The muscle tone increases and shivering may occur.
options.B: There is excessive secretion of catecholamines.
options.C: The sympathetic N.S. is activated causing cutaneous V.C. and piloerection.
options.D: Ingestion of protein food is preferred due to its high SDA.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true, but it is only one of several coordinated cold responses listed, so it is not the most complete answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (sympathetic activation raises circulating catecholamines), but it too is only one part of the full response.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (sympathetic cutaneous vasoconstriction and piloerection both reduce heat loss), but again only one part of the coordinated response.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (protein's high specific dynamic action, ~30%, generates more diet-induced heat than carbohydrate or fat), but it is one contributing factor among several.
explanations.E: Correct. Exposure to cold triggers a coordinated sympathetic response, not any single isolated change: muscle tone rises toward shivering, catecholamine secretion increases, cutaneous vasoconstriction and piloerection reduce heat loss, and protein food is physiologically preferred for its high specific dynamic action. All four of the preceding statements are true simultaneously, which is exactly why 'all of the above' is the best answer rather than any one of them alone.

questions.learning_objective: State that cold exposure produces a coordinated response: rising muscle tone/shivering, catecholamine secretion, cutaneous vasoconstriction and piloerection, and preference for high-SDA protein food.

questions.title: Evaporation: the only heat loss mechanism at all environmental temperatures
questions.question: The only heat loss mechanism that can occur in all environmental temperatures:

options.A: Radiation.
options.B: Evaporation.
options.C: Conduction.
options.D: Convection.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Radiation only moves heat from the body to the environment when the environment is cooler than the body; above body temperature it stops contributing, or reverses.
explanations.B: Correct. Evaporation depends on a humidity gradient rather than a temperature gradient, so it keeps working even when the environment is at or above body temperature, unlike radiation, conduction and convection, which all require a negative body-to-environment temperature gradient. This is why evaporation is the one mechanism that remains available at every ambient temperature, including hot environments where the other three cannot contribute to heat loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conduction, like radiation, requires the environment to be cooler than the body; it cannot move heat out of the body once that gradient disappears or reverses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Convection likewise depends on a temperature gradient between the body surface and the surrounding air or fluid, and stops contributing to heat loss once the environment is as warm as, or warmer than, the body.

questions.learning_objective: State that evaporation is the only heat-loss mechanism that remains available at every ambient temperature.

questions.title: At 38C/20% humidity, heat loss occurs by evaporation
questions.question: At an environmental temperature 38°C and humidity 20%, heat loss occurs by:

options.A: Conduction.
options.B: Radiation.
options.C: Convection.
options.D: Evaporation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. At 38C the environment is close to, or above, normal body temperature, so the gradient conduction needs to carry heat out of the body has essentially disappeared.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The same near-zero (or reversed) temperature gradient at 38C removes radiation's ability to move heat from the body to the environment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Convection likewise depends on a body-to-environment temperature gradient that is not available at 38C.
explanations.D: Correct. With the environment close to body temperature, radiation, conduction and convection all lose the gradient they depend on, leaving evaporation -- which depends on a humidity gradient, not a temperature gradient -- as the only mechanism still able to remove heat. The relatively low 20% humidity here also means the air is far from saturated, so evaporation can proceed efficiently.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the rule that evaporation dominates heat loss when ambient temperature is close to body temperature, since the other three mechanisms lose their driving gradient.

questions.title: Body temp lower than atmospheric temp: none of the listed is heat loss
questions.question: When the body temp. is lower than the atmospheric temp, heat loss occurs by:

options.A: Radiation.
options.B: Conduction.
options.C: Convection.
options.D: None of the above

explanations.A: Incorrect. If body temperature is lower than atmospheric temperature, the gradient for radiation runs from the environment into the body -- heat gain, not heat loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The same reversed gradient means conduction would carry heat into the body from the warmer environment, not out of it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Convection follows the same gradient logic and would likewise move heat into the body under these conditions.
explanations.D: Correct. Radiation, conduction and convection each move heat down whatever temperature gradient exists between the body and the environment. If the environment is warmer than the body, that gradient runs the opposite way from usual, so all three mechanisms move heat into the body (heat gain) rather than out of it, and none of them can be described as producing heat loss under this reversed condition.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a reversed body-to-environment temperature gradient turns radiation, conduction and convection into heat-gain, not heat-loss, mechanisms.

questions.title: At 15C, heat loss occurs by radiation and conduction
questions.question: When the atmospheric temp is 15°C heat loss occurs by:

options.A: Radiation and conduction.
options.B: Increased urination and defecation.
options.C: Evaporation of sweat.
options.D: Increased respiration.

explanations.A: Correct. At 15C the environment is well below normal body temperature, giving radiation and conduction (as well as convection) a substantial gradient to work with. These non-evaporative mechanisms therefore dominate heat loss in this cool, but not extreme, condition. This is unlike temperatures close to body temperature, where the gradient disappears and evaporation must take over instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Urination and defecation are excretory processes, not recognised thermoregulatory heat-loss mechanisms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sweat evaporation becomes the dominant mechanism when the environment approaches or exceeds body temperature; at a cooler 15C, the temperature-gradient mechanisms (radiation, conduction) are already sufficient and evaporation is not the primary route.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased respiration is not a major heat-loss mechanism in humans at this ambient temperature (unlike panting in some other species).

questions.learning_objective: State that at a moderately cool ambient temperature (15C), heat loss occurs mainly by radiation and conduction.

questions.title: Hot humid atmosphere: vasodilatation in skin blood vessels
questions.question: On exposure to a hot humid atmosphere:

options.A: Sweat secretion is inhibited.
options.B: V.D. occurs in the skin blood vessels.
options.C: Sweat evaporation increases
options.D: Na+ is retained in the body.
options.E: The muscle tone and secretion of thyroxine tend to increase.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sweat secretion is stimulated, not inhibited, by heat exposure -- the problem in a hot humid environment is that evaporation of that sweat is impaired, not that secretion itself is blocked.
explanations.B: Correct. In a hot atmosphere, cutaneous vasodilation increases blood flow to the skin. This brings core heat to the body surface so it can be lost by whatever gradient remains and supports evaporative loss, even though the high humidity itself blunts how effectively that sweat can actually evaporate. Vasodilation is therefore the circulatory half of the heat-loss response, working alongside sweating rather than in place of it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. High humidity impairs, rather than increases, sweat evaporation, since the surrounding air is already close to saturated with water vapour and cannot take up much more.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Heat exposure does not characteristically produce sodium retention as a direct thermoregulatory response; sweat itself contains sodium loss, if anything, rather than net retention being the defining response here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Heat exposure reduces, rather than increases, muscle tone and thyroxine-driven metabolic heat production, since both would add unwanted heat -- this is the opposite direction from the cold-exposure response.

questions.learning_objective: State that a hot humid atmosphere produces cutaneous vasodilation to support heat loss.

questions.title: Heat stroke primarily caused by inability to evaporate sweat in high humidity
questions.question: Heat stroke (hyperthermia) is primarily caused by:

options.A: Excessive heat gain by conduction.
options.B: Excessive heat production in the body.
options.C: Inability to evaporate sweat due to excessive humidity.
options.D: Inability to lose heat by radiation and other non-evaporative mechanisms.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Conduction alone is not the primary mechanism behind heat stroke; heat stroke's defining failure is evaporative, not conductive.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Heat stroke is not primarily a matter of excessive heat production -- it is the failure of the body's main heat-loss route (evaporation) that lets body temperature climb dangerously, even without unusually high heat production.
explanations.C: Correct. Heat stroke is caused primarily by the inability to evaporate sweat effectively when ambient humidity is excessive. Since evaporation depends on a dry-air gradient, high humidity blocks the body's one heat-loss mechanism that would otherwise still work even at high ambient temperatures, leaving the body with no effective way to dissipate the heat it continues to produce and gain.
explanations.D: Incorrect. In a hot environment, radiation and other non-evaporative mechanisms are already unavailable (no favourable temperature gradient); it is specifically the failure of the remaining evaporative route, not those already-unavailable mechanisms, that defines heat stroke.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Excess clothing can contribute to heat retention but is not the primary physiological cause of heat stroke; the defining mechanism is evaporative failure in high humidity.

questions.learning_objective: State that heat stroke is caused primarily by the inability to evaporate sweat due to excessive humidity.

questions.title: Hyperpyrexia mainly due to irregular central thermoregulatory mechanisms
questions.question: Elevation of the body temperature to dangerous levels (hyperpyrexia):

options.A: Is often produced as a result of excessive heat production.
options.B: Is mainly due to irregularity of the central thermoregulatory mechanisms and development of vicious circles.
options.C: Is fatal if the body temperature rises 3 °C above the normal set point.
options.D: Leads to death mainly due to renal failure and liver damage.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the main cause -- excessive heat production can contribute, but it is not the main mechanism; the defining problem in hyperpyrexia is a breakdown of the regulatory system itself, not simply making more heat.
explanations.B: Correct. Hyperpyrexia is mainly due to irregularity of the central (hypothalamic) thermoregulatory mechanisms themselves, with self-reinforcing vicious circles developing as rising temperature progressively impairs the very mechanisms that should be correcting it. This regulatory breakdown, rather than excess heat production alone, is what allows body temperature to climb to dangerous levels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. No single fixed temperature-rise threshold (such as 3C above set point) is the standard teaching definition of when hyperpyrexia becomes fatal; danger depends on the absolute temperature reached and how long it is sustained, not a fixed delta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renal failure and liver damage are not identified as the main mechanism of death in hyperpyrexia in standard teaching; cellular/enzyme damage and CNS effects are the more commonly cited dangers.

questions.learning_objective: State that hyperpyrexia is mainly due to irregularity of the central thermoregulatory mechanisms and self-reinforcing vicious circles, not excessive heat production alone.

questions.title: Eccrine sweat gland secretion can be blocked by atropine
questions.question: About the sweat glands:

options.A: They are 5 types.
options.B: The apocrine glands are responsible for temperature regulation.
options.C: The eccrine glands secrete a hypertonic solution.
options.D: The apocrine glands receive sympathetic cholinergic nerves.
options.E: The secretion of the eccrine glands can be blocked by atropine.

explanations.A: Incorrect. There are two main types of sweat gland (eccrine and apocrine), not five.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the eccrine glands, not the apocrine glands, that are the true thermoregulatory sweat glands, distributed over most of the body surface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eccrine sweat is characteristically a hypotonic, not hypertonic, fluid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the eccrine glands, not the apocrine glands, that receive sympathetic cholinergic innervation -- an unusual pairing for the sympathetic system, since most other sympathetic postganglionic fibres are adrenergic.
explanations.E: Correct. Because eccrine sweat gland secretion is driven by sympathetic cholinergic fibres, it can be blocked by atropine, an anticholinergic drug that antagonises muscarinic receptors -- exactly the receptor type these cholinergic sympathetic fibres act on. This is why anticholinergic drugs such as atropine characteristically cause anhidrosis (reduced sweating) as a side effect.

questions.learning_objective: State that eccrine sweat gland secretion, being sympathetic cholinergic, can be blocked by atropine.

field_notes.optionTrim: Source prints 6 options (A-F); the platform contract caps a question at 5. Dropped option F ("apocrine glands not responsive to oxytocin"), the least central distractor and not the correct answer -- correct letter E is unaffected.

questions.title: Endogenous pyrogen, EXCEPT: does not act via local hypothalamic histamine release
questions.question: About the endogenous pyrogen, the following is true except:

options.A: It is a protein produced by monocytes and macrophages that causes fever.
options.B: It is released by the effect of endotoxins released from pathogenic bacteria.
options.C: It resets the hypothalamic thermostat to a higher set point than normal.
options.D: It acts by increasing the local release of histamine in the hypothalamus.
options.E: It increases the heat production mechanisms specially by inducing shivering

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Endogenous pyrogen is a protein produced by monocytes and macrophages, and it is the mediator that causes fever.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Endotoxins released from pathogenic bacteria are a classic trigger for endogenous pyrogen release.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Resetting the hypothalamic thermostat to a higher set point is exactly what produces the fever response.
explanations.D: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). Endogenous pyrogen resets the hypothalamic thermostat by locally increasing the release of prostaglandins (chiefly PGE2) in the hypothalamus, not histamine -- prostaglandin is the mediator, which is exactly why aspirin (a prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitor) is an effective antipyretic. Histamine plays no defining role in this specific fever-resetting mechanism.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Once the set point is raised, the body increases heat production, especially by inducing shivering, and decreases heat loss, especially by inducing cutaneous vasoconstriction, both driving temperature up toward the new set point.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that endogenous pyrogen resets the hypothalamic thermostat via local prostaglandin, not histamine, release.

field_notes.optionTrim: Source prints 6 options (A-F); the platform contract caps a question at 5. Merged option F (decreased heat loss via cutaneous V.C.) into option E's explanation as a companion true fact, since both F and E were true, non-exception filler statements -- correct letter D is unaffected.

questions.title: Wrong statement: hyperpyrexia dangerous because it leads to heart failure
questions.question: Which of the following statements is wrong

options.A: The endogenous pyrogen causes fever accompanied by a subjective cold sensation
options.B: Aspirin produces an antipyretic effect by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
options.C: Fever is sometimes beneficial.
options.D: The endogenous pyrogen activates the heat antidrop mechanisms.
options.E: Hyperpyrexia is dangerous because it leads to heart failure.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. Because the hypothalamic set point is raised above the current body temperature, the body initially feels cold relative to that new set point, producing the subjective cold sensation (chills) that accompanies the onset of fever.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. Aspirin's antipyretic action works by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, the same local hypothalamic mediator pathway endogenous pyrogen uses to raise the set point.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. A moderate fever can be beneficial by impairing the growth of some pathogens and enhancing certain immune functions, which is part of why fever is not simply treated as purely harmful.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. Endogenous pyrogen activates the heat-gain (antidrop) mechanisms -- increased heat production and decreased heat loss -- to drive body temperature up toward the new set point.
explanations.E: Correct -- this is the wrong statement (the exception). Standard teaching attributes hyperpyrexia's danger mainly to denaturation of cellular proteins and enzymes and to central nervous system damage as body temperature climbs to extreme levels. Heart failure is not identified as the primary mechanism of danger in standard teaching, even though extreme hyperthermia can place strain on the cardiovascular system as a secondary effect. Describing heart failure as the reason hyperpyrexia is dangerous therefore overstates and misattributes the actual, primarily cellular and neurological, danger.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that hyperpyrexia's danger is not correctly described as leading primarily to heart failure.

field_notes.authorDoubt: This source does not itself state the alternative explanation (protein/enzyme denaturation and CNS damage) for why heart failure is not the standard-teaching danger of hyperpyrexia -- reasoning supplied from standard undergraduate physiology teaching rather than quoted from this bank.

questions.title: Sweat evaporation, EXCEPT: not limited to only humid climates
questions.question: Concerning sweat, all the following is true except:

options.A: The sweat secretion center is located in the anterior hypothalamic nuclei.
options.B: Its secretion starts at an atmospheric temperature of about 32-34 °C
options.C: it is an effective evaporative heat loss mechanism.
options.D: Its evaporation occurs only in humid climates
options.E: its excessive secretion leads to dehydration, salt loss and may be muscle cramps

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. The sweat secretion centre sits in the anterior hypothalamic nuclei, alongside the heat-loss centre it serves.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Sweat secretion characteristically begins once atmospheric temperature reaches about 32-34C.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Sweating is an effective evaporative heat-loss mechanism, the body's main defence against overheating.
explanations.D: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). Sweat evaporation is not limited to humid climates -- in fact, it works best and most efficiently in a dry (low-humidity) climate, where the surrounding air is far from saturated with water vapour and can readily absorb more. High humidity, if anything, impairs sweat evaporation, which is exactly the mechanism behind heat stroke in hot, humid environments.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Excessive sweat secretion causes fluid and salt loss, which can lead to dehydration and, in some cases, muscle cramps (as in heat/miner's cramps).

questions.learning_objective: Identify that sweat evaporation is impaired, not enabled, by a humid climate.

questions.title: EXCEPT: heat-loss and heat-gain centre activation is reversed in the false statement
questions.question: All the following statements are true except

options.A: In the comfortable zone of environmental temp., the body temp. is kept constant only by the non-evaporative heat loss mechanisms.
options.B: Miner's cramps can be treated by giving salt tablets.
options.C: The heat-loss center is located in the anterior hypothalamic nuclei and it produces temp. antirise responses mainly via physical processes.
options.D: The heat-gain center is located in the posterior hypothalamic nuclei and it produces temp. antidrop responses mainly via chemical processes.
options.E: The heat-loss center is stimulated in cold weather while the heat-gain center is stimulated in hot weather.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Within the thermally comfortable zone, the small ongoing heat-loss needed to balance basal heat production is handled by non-evaporative mechanisms (radiation, conduction, convection), without needing sweating.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Miner's cramps, caused by excessive salt loss through profuse sweating, are treated by replacing that lost salt with salt tablets.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. The heat-loss centre sits in the anterior hypothalamic nuclei and drives antirise (cooling) responses mainly through physical mechanisms such as vasodilation and sweating.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. The heat-gain centre sits in the posterior hypothalamic nuclei and drives antidrop (warming) responses mainly through chemical mechanisms such as increased metabolic heat production and shivering.
explanations.E: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). This reverses the true pairing between each centre and the weather that activates it. The heat-loss centre is stimulated when the body needs to lose heat, that is, in hot weather, not cold. The heat-gain centre is stimulated when the body needs to gain heat, that is, in cold weather, not hot -- the opposite of what this statement claims for both centres.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the heat-loss centre is stimulated in hot weather and the heat-gain centre in cold weather, not the reverse.

questions.title: Body temperature: all listed statements true
questions.question: About the body temperature:

options.A: Its regulation is given the priority in homeostasis.
options.B: In very hot environments, it can be efficiently unaltered by wetting the skin by cold water.
options.C: Evaporation of one ml of sweat leads to heat loss of about 0.6 Kcal.
options.D: Atropine increases it while curare decreases it.
options.E: All of the above are true.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true, but it is only one of several true statements listed, so it is not the most complete answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (wetting the skin with cold water helps keep body temperature stable in very hot environments by supplementing evaporative and conductive cooling), but only one part of the full set.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (evaporating about 1 mL of sweat removes roughly 0.6 Kcal of heat), but again only one part.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (atropine, by blocking sweating, raises body temperature; curare, by abolishing muscle-tone-driven heat production, lowers it), but only one part.
explanations.E: Correct. Each of the preceding statements about body temperature regulation is independently true: its priority in homeostasis, the efficiency of wetting the skin in extreme heat, the heat removed per millilitre of sweat evaporated, and the opposite effects of atropine and curare. Since all four are correct, 'all of the above' is the best answer rather than singling out any one of them.

questions.learning_objective: State that body temperature regulation has homeostatic priority, that wetting the skin helps in extreme heat, the heat removed per mL of sweat evaporated, and the opposite effects of atropine and curare on body temperature.

questions.title: Ingestion of protein meals causes marked increase in metabolic rate
questions.question: Ingestion of protein meals.

options.A: Causes a marked increase in the metabolic rate.
options.B: Is preferable in hot climate.
options.C: Leads to decreased urea formation in the liver.
options.D: Decreases the synthesis of essential amino acids in the liver.
options.E: Causes the liver to derive its energy needs from oxidation of fatty acids.

explanations.A: Correct. Protein has by far the largest specific dynamic action of the three foodstuffs, about 30%, driven mainly by the metabolic cost of processing absorbed amino acids (chiefly deamination) in the liver. This is why ingesting a protein meal causes a marked, noticeably larger rise in metabolic rate than an equivalent carbohydrate (~6%) or fat (~4%) meal would.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because protein generates the most diet-induced heat (the largest SDA), it is preferable in cold, not hot, climates, where that extra heat is welcome rather than a burden.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Protein metabolism increases, rather than decreases, urea formation in the liver, since deaminated amino acids' nitrogen is disposed of as urea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ingested protein supplies amino acids the liver can use, rather than decreasing the liver's synthesis of essential amino acids -- and in any case, essential amino acids by definition cannot be synthesised by the body and must come from the diet.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Following a protein meal, the liver has abundant amino-acid substrate freshly available and is not characteristically shifted toward deriving its energy needs from fatty acid oxidation as the defining response to protein ingestion.

questions.subtopic: Basal metabolic rate and specific dynamic action
questions.learning_objective: State that protein ingestion causes a marked increase in metabolic rate, reflecting its large specific dynamic action relative to carbohydrate or fat.

field_notes.ownConceptReuse: Reuses CON-FND-BA8CBB467C0506 (lane2's BMR/SDA concept, already stating protein's ~30% SDA) rather than minting a new record -- the same fact tested from a different stem angle.

questions.title: After 1 week starvation, urine contains excess NH3 and pH drops
questions.question: After one week of starvation:

options.A: The respiratory quotient becomes about 1.
options.B: The blood glucose level is much decreased below the fasting level.
options.C: The urine contains an excessive amount of NH3 and its pH drops.
options.D: The main source of energy is the liver glycogen.
options.E: The serum lipid level is not significantly changed.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The respiratory quotient falls, not rises toward 1, as starvation progresses, since the body shifts increasingly toward fat oxidation, whose RQ is lower (~0.7) than carbohydrate's.
explanations.B: Incorrect. After the initial fall, blood glucose is defended relatively well by gluconeogenesis (from amino acids and, later, glycerol) and is not much further decreased below the fasting level by one week.
explanations.C: Correct. By about one week into starvation, fat-derived ketone bodies have accumulated enough to produce a mounting metabolic acidosis. The kidney responds by increasingly excreting hydrogen ion as ammonium to buffer this acidosis. This shift shows up directly in the urine as an excessive amount of ammonia and a fall in urinary pH.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Liver glycogen stores are largely depleted within about 24 hours of fasting, far too early to still be the main energy source a full week into starvation; fat becomes the dominant fuel well before this point.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Serum lipid (free fatty acid and ketone body) levels rise significantly during starvation, as fat mobilisation becomes the dominant source of energy.

questions.learning_objective: State that after about one week of starvation, urinary ammonia rises and urinary pH falls as the kidney buffers ketoacidosis.

questions.title: False during starvation: plasma protein concentration decreases
questions.question: It is false that during starvation:

options.A: The blood glucose level remains constant at the fasting level.
options.B: There is lipaemia and ketosis.
options.C: The plasma protein concentration decreases.
options.D: The amount of the alkali reserve is decreased.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the false statement -- this statement is true. Blood glucose is relatively well defended near the fasting level by gluconeogenesis during starvation.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the false statement -- this statement is true. As fat mobilisation becomes the dominant fuel source, both lipaemia (raised blood lipids) and ketosis (accumulating ketone bodies) develop.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the false statement (the exception). The body preferentially spares plasma protein during starvation, breaking down other, more expendable protein, chiefly skeletal muscle, first. Plasma protein concentration is therefore relatively protected rather than falling, at least through the earlier and moderate phases of starvation. This protein-sparing pattern is exactly what distinguishes starvation from a state of true protein deficiency, where plasma protein does fall.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the false statement -- this statement is true. The developing ketoacidosis of starvation consumes the body's alkali (bicarbonate) buffering reserve, decreasing it.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the false statement -- this statement is true. Blood volume is relatively well maintained (protected by the same homeostatic priority mechanisms) during starvation, compared with the more marked changes in fuel stores and electrolytes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that plasma protein concentration is relatively spared, not decreased, during starvation, unlike muscle protein.

questions.title: Starvation: all listed statements true
questions.question: During starvation:

options.A: The body gets energy first from carbohydrates then from fat and finally from proteins.
options.B: Protein catabolism is unavoidable from the start.
options.C: The blood levels of most electrolytes remain fairly constant.
options.D: Signs of vitamin deficiency and acidosis develop as starvation advances.
options.E: All of the above is true

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (carbohydrate stores are used first, then fat becomes dominant, and protein breakdown intensifies late), but it is only one of several true statements listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (the brain's obligatory glucose need must be met by gluconeogenesis from amino acids from the very start, before ketone-body adaptation is established, so some protein catabolism is unavoidable even while fat becomes the dominant fuel), but only one part of the full set.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (most electrolyte levels are relatively well maintained by homeostatic priority), but only one part.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (as reserves are progressively exhausted, both vitamin deficiency and worsening acidosis develop), but only one part.
explanations.E: Correct. Each of the preceding statements about starvation is independently true: the sequential order of substrate use, the unavoidable early protein catabolism needed to fuel the brain, the relative stability of most electrolytes, and the progressive development of vitamin deficiency and acidosis. The bank's own printed source also states, as a companion fact not separately re-tested here, that the brain and heart are relatively spared functionally until the terminal stage of starvation. Since these statements are correct and mutually compatible, 'all of the above' is the best answer.

questions.learning_objective: State the pattern of starvation metabolism: substrate-use order, early obligatory protein catabolism, electrolyte stability, and progressive vitamin deficiency and acidosis; brain/heart sparing is taught as a companion fact by the same concept.

questions.title: Obesity, EXCEPT: not produced by excess protein deposition
questions.question: About obesity, all the following is true except:

options.A: It is the commonest nutritional disorder.
options.B: It is associated with a fall in the body's specific gravity.
options.C: It is produced by deposition of excess protein in the body.
options.D: It occurs as a result of +ve energy balance often due to hyperphagia.
options.E: Psychogenic, genetic and hypothalamic abnormalities may be causative factors.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Obesity is generally regarded as the commonest nutritional disorder in many populations.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Since fat tissue is less dense than lean tissue, an increased proportion of body fat lowers the body's overall specific gravity.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). Obesity reflects a sustained positive energy balance. It is characterised by increased deposition of fat, not protein, in the body. Excess protein deposition is not the mechanism of obesity, unlike the excess fat storage that actually defines it.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Obesity results from a sustained positive energy balance, often driven by hyperphagia (excessive food intake relative to expenditure).
explanations.E: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Psychogenic, genetic and hypothalamic abnormalities are all recognised contributing causative factors in obesity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that obesity is produced by excess fat, not protein, deposition, extending the same energy-balance concept to the specific case of obesity.

field_notes.ownConceptReuse: Reuses CON-FND-8027C14DF87022 (lane2's energy-balance concept), which already states that obesity reflects increased fat, not protein, content -- extends its exam_weight/original_wording rather than minting a duplicate obesity concept.

questions.title: Appetite, EXCEPT: not completely lost after gastrectomy
questions.question: Concerning the appetite, all the following is true except:

options.A: It is affected by certain hypothalamic areas.
options.B: It is completely lost after gastrectomy.
options.C: It is reduced if the stomach is over distended.
options.D: It increases as the blood glucose level falls.
options.E: It increases on exposure to cold climates.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Appetite is governed mainly by hypothalamic centres integrating several inputs.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). Gastrectomy removes the stomach's own distension and hormonal signalling, one input to appetite regulation. It does not, however, completely abolish appetite, since the hypothalamic centres themselves remain intact. The other, non-gastric inputs to those centres, such as blood glucose and ambient temperature, continue to drive appetite even without a stomach.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Gastric over-distension is one of the inputs that reduces appetite.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. A falling blood glucose level is a classic hypothalamic trigger that increases appetite.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Cold exposure increases appetite, part of the same drive that favours high-SDA protein food in cold weather.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that appetite is reduced, but not completely abolished, by gastrectomy.

questions.title: Metabolic rate can be estimated from RQ and O2 consumption
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: The metabolic rate can be estimated if the R.Q. and O2 consumption are known.
options.B: One gram of protein gives the same amount of energy whether it is oxidized in a bomb calorimeter or metabolized inside the body
options.C: The specific dynamic action persists for about 2 days after food ingestion.
options.D: The nitrogen balance is more negative in early than in late starvation.
options.E: An increase in the body fat content causes reduction of the lean body mass.

explanations.A: Correct. This is the principle behind indirect calorimetry. Once the respiratory quotient, which identifies which fuel is being oxidised, and the volume of O2 consumed are both known, the corresponding energy equivalent of oxygen for that fuel mix can be applied. This lets the metabolic rate be calculated without needing to measure heat output directly, as direct calorimetry would.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein's physical heat value (bomb calorimeter, ~5.3 Kcal/g) is higher than its physiological heat value (~4.1 Kcal/g metabolised inside the body), because the body cannot fully oxidise protein's nitrogen-containing portion and excretes it as urea -- the two values are not equal, unlike for carbohydrate and fat.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Specific dynamic action is a relatively short-lived rise in metabolic rate following a meal, lasting on the order of hours, not persisting for about two days.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nitrogen balance is generally more negative later, not earlier, in prolonged starvation as protein catabolism intensifies, rather than being worse at the very start.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An increase in fat content does not, by itself, cause a reduction in lean body mass -- the two compartments (fat mass and lean mass) can each change relatively independently, and gaining fat does not mechanistically shrink lean tissue.

questions.learning_objective: State that the metabolic rate can be estimated from the respiratory quotient together with O2 consumption (indirect calorimetry).

field_notes.ownConceptReuse: Reuses CON-FND-481FB61C091AAE (lane2's RQ concept) as main concept, with CON-FND-5948B69A224D33 (heat value/O2 equivalent) as contextual, rather than minting a new record for this indirect-calorimetry restatement.

questions.title: Obesity wrong statement: amphetamine is not useful since it increases appetite
questions.question: Which of the following statements about obesity is wrong?

options.A: Obesity may be hypertrophic or hyperplastic-hypertrophic.
options.B: Some cases of obesity are due to resetting of the hypothalamic appestat to a higher level than normal.
options.C: Obesity is present when more than 20% of the body weight is due to fat in males and more than 25% in females.
options.D: The use of diuretics and thyroxine for reducing the body weight is not advisable due to their harmful effects
options.E: Amphetamine is not useful in its treatment since it increases the appetite.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. Obesity is classified by whether it involves enlargement of existing fat cells (hypertrophic) or an increase in fat cell number as well (hyperplastic-hypertrophic).
explanations.B: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. In some cases obesity is driven by resetting of the hypothalamic appestat to a higher-than-normal level, sustaining excess intake.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. These are the standard teaching thresholds for defining obesity by percentage body fat in males and females.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the wrong statement -- this statement is true. Diuretics and thyroxine are not advisable for weight reduction because of their harmful effects (fluid/electrolyte disturbance and thyrotoxic effects, respectively), despite any transient weight change they might produce.
explanations.E: Correct -- this is the wrong statement (the exception). Amphetamine is used as an anti-obesity agent precisely because it suppresses, not increases, appetite. Its central stimulant action includes an anorexiant effect on the hypothalamic appetite centres, which is the actual basis of its clinical usefulness in obesity treatment. Describing it as unhelpful because it increases appetite therefore reverses its real pharmacology.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that amphetamine is useful in obesity treatment because it suppresses, not increases, appetite.

questions.title: Cell membrane, EXCEPT: does not have a monolipid layer
questions.question: Regarding the cell membrane are all true, EXCEPT:

options.A: has integral proteins which form channels
options.B: has peripheral proteins that act as receptors
options.C: has a monolipid layer.
options.D: allow diffusion of O2 and CO2

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Integral proteins span or embed within the bilayer and form the membrane's channels.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Peripheral proteins sit on the membrane surface and act as receptors, among other roles.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). The cell membrane's lipid component is a bilayer, two layers of phospholipid, not a single (mono) lipid layer. This bilayer arrangement, with hydrophobic tails facing inward and hydrophilic heads facing outward on both sides, is what gives the membrane its selective permeability. A monolayer would not provide this same barrier structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Small lipid-soluble gases such as O2 and CO2 diffuse directly through the lipid bilayer.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the cell membrane's lipid component is a bilayer, not a monolayer.

questions.title: Membrane proteins act as receptors for hormones
questions.question: Among functions of proteins in the cell membrane:

options.A: to carry metals and hormones.
options.B: to act as receptors for hormones.
options.C: to allow diffusion from extracellular space to inside cells against concentration and electrical gradient.
options.D: integral proteins are needed for active transport of glucose into cells.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carrying metals and hormones as the defining function is not the standard teaching description of membrane protein function tested here; acting as a receptor is the better, more precise description.
explanations.B: Correct. A key function of membrane proteins, specifically peripheral proteins on the membrane surface, is to act as receptors. Hormones bind to these receptors to produce their effects on the cell. This receptor role is essential for water-soluble hormones, which cannot cross the lipid bilayer directly and so depend entirely on a surface receptor to signal into the cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Diffusion... against concentration and electrical gradient" is a contradiction in terms -- diffusion by definition moves down a gradient; movement against a gradient is active transport, not diffusion, so this option misdescribes the mechanism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucose normally crosses the cell membrane by facilitated diffusion (a passive, carrier-mediated process, e.g. via GLUT transporters), not active transport, under ordinary physiological conditions.

questions.learning_objective: State that membrane proteins, specifically peripheral proteins, act as receptors for hormones.

questions.title: Internal environment has Na+ as its major cation
questions.question: The internal environment:

options.A: has Na+ as its major cation.
options.B: is the fluid found in cell.
options.C: normally has a pH of 7.0.
options.D: has a protein content greater than that of plasma.

explanations.A: Correct. The internal environment is the extracellular fluid (ECF). Sodium is its major cation, present at a far higher concentration in the ECF than inside cells. Inside cells, potassium is instead the dominant cation, a reciprocal distribution the Na+-K+ pump actively maintains.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal environment is the extracellular fluid, the fluid surrounding cells, not the fluid found inside cells (which is the intracellular fluid, ICF).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Normal extracellular fluid (blood/plasma) pH is about 7.4, slightly alkaline, not 7.0.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option describes a fluid with a higher protein content than plasma, which is the reverse of the ECF's own subcompartments -- plasma itself has a higher protein concentration than the interstitial fluid that makes up most of the rest of the ECF, not lower.

questions.learning_objective: State that sodium is the major cation of the internal environment (extracellular fluid).

questions.title: Cell membrane contains peripheral proteins that bind hormones
questions.question: The cell membrane contains:

options.A: peripheral proteins to which hormones can bind to produce their effects.
options.B: lipids which prevent the diffusion of respiratory gases between extracellular and intracellular fluid.
options.C: integral proteins which are important for the transport of fat soluble molecules.
options.D: an energy-dependent transport process by which K+ ions are normally removed from the cell.

explanations.A: Correct. Peripheral proteins on the membrane surface are the site hormones bind to produce their effects. This receptor role is essential since most hormones, especially water-soluble ones, cannot cross the lipid bilayer directly to act inside the cell. Binding a surface peripheral protein instead lets the hormone trigger an intracellular signal without itself entering the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Membrane lipids do not prevent respiratory gas diffusion -- small lipid-soluble gases such as O2 and CO2 in fact diffuse readily through the lipid bilayer, which is precisely how they cross the membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fat-soluble molecules typically cross the membrane directly through the lipid bilayer itself, without needing an integral transport protein; it is water-soluble, not fat-soluble, molecules that generally need protein-mediated transport.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The physiological energy-dependent pump (the Na+-K+ pump) normally pumps K+ into, not out of, the cell (while pumping Na+ out) -- this option reverses the pump's actual direction for potassium.

questions.learning_objective: State that peripheral membrane proteins are the site hormones bind to produce their effects.

questions.title: Cell membrane peripheral proteins function as enzymes or hormone receptors
questions.question: The cell membrane contains:

options.A: peripheral proteins which may function as enzymes or hormone receptors.
options.B: integral proteins which are necessary for the transport of respiratory gases.
options.C: channels through which alcohol can diffuse easily.
options.D: two layers of proteins.

explanations.A: Correct. Peripheral proteins sit on the membrane surface rather than spanning the bilayer the way integral proteins do. From that surface position, they may function either as enzymes catalysing reactions at the membrane, or as receptors for hormones and other signalling molecules. Both roles depend on the protein staying accessible at the surface rather than being embedded within the lipid bilayer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Respiratory gases (O2, CO2) cross the membrane by simple diffusion directly through the lipid bilayer; they do not require integral transport proteins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alcohol, being small and lipid-soluble, diffuses directly through the lipid bilayer itself rather than through dedicated protein channels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The membrane's structural framework is a phospholipid bilayer (two layers of lipid), not two layers of protein; proteins are embedded in or attached to that lipid bilayer, not arranged as a separate double protein layer.

questions.learning_objective: State that peripheral membrane proteins may function as enzymes or hormone receptors.

questions.title: The internal body environment refers to the ECF
questions.question: the internal body environment refers to:

options.A: ICF
options.B: ECG
options.C: ECF
options.D: organs

explanations.A: Incorrect. ICF (intracellular fluid) is the fluid inside cells; the internal environment classically refers to the fluid surrounding cells, the extracellular fluid, not the fluid within them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ECG (electrocardiogram) is a recording of the heart's electrical activity, unrelated to the internal-environment concept this question tests.
explanations.C: Correct. The internal body environment, in the classical (Claude Bernard) sense, refers to the extracellular fluid (ECF). This is the fluid that directly bathes the body's cells, distinct from the fluid inside them. The body's homeostatic mechanisms work continuously to keep the composition of this ECF constant, which is exactly what the term "internal environment" is meant to capture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Organs are structures, not a fluid compartment, and are not what the term "internal environment" refers to.

questions.learning_objective: State that the internal body environment refers to the extracellular fluid (ECF).

field_notes.crossQuestionNote: Same concept as Q115 (this same batch) -- Q115 asks for the ECF's major cation, this asks what the internal environment itself is; not a duplicate, the concept's own field_notes already flags the pairing.
